case_prompt: A 42-year-old Asian woman presented with a 5-day history of fever and chills and a 2-day history of jaundice. Three months earlier she had undergone laparoscopic cholecystectomy for cholangitis due to gallstones. She had no family history of hemolytic disease. On examination, she was alert, temperature 39.3 °C, blood pressure 122/61 mmHg, pulse 119 beats/min, and respiration rate normal; skin and sclera were icteric, with no abdominal or costovertebral-angle tenderness. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL, reticulocyte count 25.0%, white-cell count 10,580/µL, platelets 125,000/µL; total bilirubin 10.9 mg/dL (direct 6.0 mg/dL), AST 49 IU/L, ALT 65 IU/L, ALP 441 IU/L, LDH 550 IU/L, and GGT 301 IU/L; coagulation tests were normal. Blood cultures grew Escherichia coli. Abdominal contrast CT revealed splenomegaly and a distended left kidney, with no biliary-tract obstruction. Urinalysis showed leukocyte esterase 3+, nitrite 2+, hemoglobin 3+, bilirubin 2+, and urobilinogen 3+; sediment contained white cells, bacteria, and 5–9 erythrocytes per high-power field, and urine culture grew E. coli. Further testing showed haptoglobin 8 mg/dL and negative direct and indirect Coombs tests. A peripheral blood smear revealed spherocytes.

sentences.text: A 42-year-old Asian woman presented with a 5-day history of fever and chills and a 2-day history of jaundice.
Three months earlier she had undergone laparoscopic cholecystectomy for cholangitis due to gallstones.
She had no family history of hemolytic disease.

On examination, she was alert, temperature 39.3 °C, blood pressure 122/61 mmHg, pulse 119 beats/min, and respiration rate normal; skin and sclera were icteric, with no abdominal or costovertebral-angle tenderness.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL, reticulocyte count 25.0%, white-cell count 10,580/µL, platelets 125,000/µL; total bilirubin 10.9 mg/dL (direct 6.0 mg/dL), AST 49 IU/L, ALT 65 IU/L, ALP 441 IU/L, LDH 550 IU/L, and GGT 301 IU/L; coagulation tests were normal. Blood cultures grew Escherichia coli.
Abdominal contrast CT revealed splenomegaly and a distended left kidney, with no biliary-tract obstruction.

Urinalysis showed leukocyte esterase 3+, nitrite 2+, hemoglobin 3+, bilirubin 2+, and urobilinogen 3+; sediment contained white cells, bacteria, and 5–9 erythrocytes per high-power field, and urine culture grew E. coli.
Further testing showed haptoglobin 8 mg/dL and negative direct and indirect Coombs tests.
A peripheral blood smear revealed spherocytes.

diagnostic_reasoning: 1. Acute obstructive suppurative cholangitis was considered because of fever, jaundice, and elevated liver‐function tests, but it was excluded because “no signs of biliary tract obstruction were present.” 2. Pyelonephritis was suggested by the urine findings and imaging, as “urinalysis findings suggested the diagnosis of septicemia due to pyelonephritis; however, the cause of the patient’s hyperbilirubinemia was unclear.” 3. Other infections accompanied with hyperbilirubinemia, such as infectious mononucleosis, malaria, and Weil syndrome (leptospirosis), were deemed unlikely because “other infections … were unlikely in light of negative findings of the microbiological examination and peripheral blood smear.” 4. Autoimmune hemolytic anemia was excluded because “the results of direct and indirect Coombs tests were negative.” 5. Hereditary spherocytosis was strongly suspected on the basis of “peripheral blood smear findings, splenomegaly and the patient’s past history of cholelithiasis.”

selection.screen_reason: Coombs-negative haemolysis with spherocytes, splenomegaly and earlier gallstones, unmasked by E. coli pyelonephritis, supports hereditary spherocytosis.
selection.second_look_note: Earlier gallstone cholangitis is the history clue behind Coombs-negative hemolysis with spherocytes and splenomegaly unmasked by E. coli pyelonephritis.
